claims.text: Very high configurational entropy at elevated temperature maintains structural and chemical stability in high-entropy nanoalloys by suppressing local ordering and clustering.
The suppression of local ordering by configurational entropy is especially strong when high-melting refractory elements are present.
Configurational entropy dominates chemical pair interactions that would otherwise cause phase separation or ordering.
Entropy stabilization is reflected in a disordered, single-phase structure that is typically BCC.
A near-equiatomic Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy with a minor Al or other high-melting addition can be taken initially as a disordered BCC solid solution.
Chemical pair interactions can promote clustering or ordering in Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni-type high-entropy alloys.
At high temperature, maximized configurational entropy statistically favors a uniform solid solution by offsetting pairwise chemical interactions.
Adding high-melting refractory elements elevates the alloy melting point and stabilizes a single high-entropy phase.
High melting points of constituent elements, which are often refractory BCC elements, are a major driving force for single-phase HEA formation.
Near-melting high-entropy alloys have a strong tendency to form BCC single-phase solid solutions.
Nanoalloys annealed at 0.8–0.95 Tm will retain a single-phase disordered BCC structure with minimal local ordering.
Otherwise similar alloys with less refractory content will exhibit more chemical ordering or phase separation after high-temperature annealing.
Lower-temperature annealing will produce more chemical ordering or phase separation than annealing at 0.8–0.95 Tm.
The proposed entropy-dominated stability regime is bounded to approximately 80–95% of the melting temperature.
Dropping below the proposed temperature range may allow enthalpy-driven ordering to dominate.
External mechanical stress may induce ordering transitions and invalidate the prediction.
XRD, TEM/SAED, and DSC can be used to distinguish phase constitution, local ordering or clustering, and phase-transition temperatures in the proposed comparison.
